name: Great Lakes kingdoms (Buganda, Bunyoro, Rwanda, Burundi)
summary: Powerful kingdoms between the African Great Lakes, among them Buganda, Bunyoro-Kitara, Nkore, Rwanda and Burundi, with royal courts, drum regalia and large armies; they came under British and German rule in the 1890s.

knownFor.label: Kasubi Tombs
knownFor.note: Tombs of the Kabakas of Buganda.

knownFor.label: Bark cloth
knownFor.note: Made from fig-tree bark in Buganda.

location.value: Buganda is in Uganda’s Central Region: Lake Victoria to the south, the Victoria Nile to the east, Lake Kyoga to the north, Ankole to the west and the River Kafu to the north-west.

terrain.value: Fertile highlands, rolling hills and the shores of Lake Victoria and other great lakes.

climate.value: Mild and rainy, with two wet seasons.

resources.value: Bananas, cattle, iron, salt and farmland.

disasters.value: Rinderpest killed most cattle in the 1890s, causing famine.

population.value: The article gives 14 million Baganda (about 16% of Uganda’s population); a later section projects about 11,952,600 in 2021.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Long, older movements of farmers and herders created the region’s mixed peoples.

economicBase.value: Farming was the backbone of Buganda's economy, with bananas as the staple that supported a dense population. Cattle herding in Rwanda and Nkore is not covered by this page.

tradeRoutes.value: Ivory and slave caravans to the Swahili coast (1840s–).

wealth.value: Royal wealth in cattle; neighbouring kingdoms paid tribute (Busoga sent slaves, goats and cattle; Ankole sent large herds). No royal cattle counts are given.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: Buganda is today a constitutional monarchy under the Kabaka (Muwenda Mutebi II since the kingdom's restoration in 1993). Rwanda and Nkore were not checked.

keyRulers.value: Muwenda Mutebi II, the 36th Kabaka, crowned on 24 July 1993. The article gives no reign dates for Mutesa I.

succession.value: Royal clans chose rulers, and succession wars were common.

institutions.value: The Lukiiko council in Buganda, chiefs and ministers in other kingdoms.

stability.value: Strong states with frequent wars among rivals.

eliteConflict.value: Princes and chiefs competed for the throne and for land.

armyAndTech.value: Spear armies and, in Buganda, large war canoes on Lake Victoria.

majorWars.value: Mutesa I’s reign was “the zenith of Ganda military power”, with sixty-six wars in twenty-eight years.

territoryChange.value: Buganda grew at Bunyoro’s expense in the 1700s and 1800s.

alliancesRivals.value: Buganda and Bunyoro were long-standing rivals.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade with Swahili and Arab traders, and later with Europeans.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, lake canoes and drum messages carried news.

religion.value: Buganda's largest faiths are Catholicism, Anglicanism, Islam and the traditional Kiganda religion. The page gives no arrival dates and does not mention the Uganda Martyrs.

artsArchitecture.value: Large grass-thatched palaces and royal tombs, such as those at Kasubi.

socialStructure.value: Royal clans, chiefs, farmers and herders.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the royal courts, clan ties and the sacred king.

dailyLife.value: Families farmed bananas and kept cattle in villages, and courts held great ceremonies.

neighbours.value: Each other, and Swahili traders on the east.

ideasReligions.value: Sacred kingship, with the king as a link between people and the spirit world.

colonisation.value: Buganda became the centre of the Uganda Protectorate in 1884 (the article’s date); the Buganda Agreements of 1900, 1955 and 1961.

riseSignals.value: Buganda was likely founded between the 12th and 14th centuries; oral tradition names Kintu as founder.

peakPeriod.value: The page calls Mutesa I's reign the zenith of Ganda military power, with sixty-six wars in twenty-eight years; it does not give his dates.

declineSignals.value: Colonial rule in the 1890s, by Britain and Germany.

outcome.value: The Kabakaship was abolished in 1967 and restored in 1993; Buganda is now a constitutional monarchy with a largely ceremonial role.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
